questions.title: What exactly does third‑party consent to a home search entail under the Fourth Amendment?
questions.question_body: In United States v. Jaison Coleman the court held that Lisa, the spouse of the defendant, could give valid consent to police entry even though Coleman was not present. How is this principle established, and what are the limits on a third party’s authority to consent to a search of a private home?

questions.title: Which factors does a court consider when determining if consent was voluntarily given?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites Bumper, Han, and several other cases that use a 'totality of the circumstances' test to assess voluntariness. What specific factors are weighed in that calculation, and how do they interact to produce a conclusion that the consent was 'free and voluntary'?  Also, how does the presence of a police officer influence that assessment?

questions.title: Does using the word 'need' in a request for entry constitute coercion?
questions.question_body: Coleman’s argument focuses on Officer Kizer’s utterance ‘I’m sensing that we almost need to come inside.’ The court dismisses this as non‑coercive. Under what circumstances might language that implies urgency or necessity be seen as coercive, and why was it found not to be in this case?

questions.title: How is the 'scope of consent' defined and applied after a police officer has entered a home?
questions.question_body: The court notes that the officers’ actions after entry were within the scope of Lisa’s consent. What exactly does 'scope of consent' mean, and what standard – such as the objective reasonableness test – does a court use to decide whether officers went beyond what the consenter intended?

questions.title: When can exigent circumstances override the need for consent, and why are they not relevant here?
questions.question_body: The opinion briefly considers whether exigent circumstances or inevitable discovery justified the officers’ entry, but ultimately rejects those grounds. What constitutes an exigent circumstance under the Fourth Amendment, and what facts in this case would have needed to be present for the doctrine to apply?

questions.title: What is the appellate standard for reviewing a district court’s findings of voluntariness and scope of consent?
questions.question_body: The court says it reviews these findings for 'clear error.' How is clear error defined in Fourth Amendment cases, and what balance does an appellate court strike between deference to the trial judge’s factual findings and the need to correct mistaken conclusions?
